segments.caption: Netflix, Gmail, Swiggy, your bank's fraud alert. Almost all of it runs on just 12 machine learning algorithms.
Here's every one, explained in under 3 minutes. Save this before your next interview.
First, the map.

Supervised algorithms learn from examples with answers. They predict a number, or a category. Unsupervised ones find patterns with no answers given. And reinforcement learning learns by trial and reward.
Number 1: linear regression.
It draws the straight line that best fits your data. Bigger flat, higher rent. Use it to predict a number.
Number 2: logistic regression.
Despite the name, it answers yes or no questions. It squeezes everything into a probability between 0 and 1. Will this customer buy? 80%, yes.
Number 3: decision tree.
A flowchart of yes or no questions. Salary above 50,000? Any existing loans? Approve, or reject.
Number 4: random forest.
One tree can be wrong. So build hundreds, each on a slightly different slice of the data, and let them vote. Banks use it to catch fraud.
Number 5: gradient boosting, like XGBoost.
Trees are built one after another, and each new tree fixes the mistakes of the last one. It wins most competitions on table data.
Number 6: K nearest neighbours.
To label a new point, look at its closest neighbours, and copy the majority. You are who your neighbours are.
Number 7: naive Bayes.
It counts how often words appear in spam versus normal mail. Free, winner, urgent? Probably spam. Great for text.
Number 8: support vector machine.
It draws the widest possible street between two classes. The points touching the edge of the street are the support vectors.
Number 9: K-means clustering.
No answers given. It drops K centres, gives each point to the nearest one, and moves the centres until the groups settle. Perfect for customer segments.
Number 10: PCA, principal component analysis.
It squeezes 100 columns into a few that keep most of the information. Faster models, easier plots.
Number 11: neural networks.
Layers of tiny calculators, each passing signals forward. Stack enough layers, and you get deep learning: face unlock, translation, ChatGPT.
Number 12: reinforcement learning.
An agent tries actions, gets rewards or penalties, and slowly learns the best moves. That's how AI mastered chess and Go.

So which one should you use? Predicting a number? Linear regression, or gradient boosting. Yes or no? Logistic regression, or a random forest. Finding groups? K means. Too many columns? PCA. Images or text? Neural networks.
